extracted.intended_audience: general readers; improvisational actors, teachers, directors, and theatre educators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for teaching and performing improvisational theatre using Viola Spolin's Theater Games: how to structure exercises, coach players (especially children), and elicit spontaneous creative performance. Emphasis on focus, game-forms, audience participation, and nonjudgmental learning environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theater Games: give players a specific focus or technical problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Spolin's Theater Games are structured to give the players a specific focus or technical problem to keep in mind during the game, "like keeping your eye on the ball in a ball game."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each game provides a concrete, operational structure that directs performer attention to a single task so they learn a theatrical skill through play. The page notes there are approximately 220 games in Improvisation for the Theater illustrating this approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on the present moment
rubrics_metrics.description: The intention of giving the actor something on which to focus is to help them to be in the present moment, like a mantra in meditation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keeping attention on the game's focus helps players produce spontaneous, intuitive choices and prevents pre-planning, comparing, or judging choices during improvisation. Focus is repeatedly emphasized as central to Spolin's method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid self-consciousness and intellectual pre-planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Games are designed so players 'learn the skill, keeping their attention on the focus of the game, rather than falling into self-consciousness or trying to think up good ideas, from an intellectual source.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-designed game occupies the player's mind with an immediate task; anti-patterns include over-intellectualizing, self-judgment, or attempting to craft clever ideas instead of responding in the moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Side-coaching (active guidance during games)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of Spolin's three core features for working with children is side-coaching—the practice of coaching players from the side while they play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Side-coaching is used to plan activities and to support players in the moment without interrupting play; it's presented as a tool for creating a productive learning space, especially with children and novices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation framed to avoid judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Spolin used 'evaluation' (one of her three core features) to create a productive safe space 'in which they were not judged based upon assumptions, but rather what they displayed in the educational environment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation in Spolin's pedagogy emphasizes observing and responding to what the player demonstrates rather than imposing assumptions about ability; scoring/assessment should be descriptive and non-shaming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcome the Approval/Disapproval Syndrome
rubrics_metrics.description: Spolin emphasized the need for the individual to overcome what she called 'The Approval/Disapproval Syndrome,' described as the performer blocking their own natural creativity in an effort to please the audience, director, teacher, peers or anyone else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers should design exercises and classroom norms that reduce performers' need for external approval so their creativity can emerge freely. Anti-patterns include praise/critique practices that reinforce performers' desire to please rather than explore.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use audience suggestions as the base of improvisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Spolin drew on J.L. Moreno's idea of using audience suggestions as the base of an improvisation; this became a hallmark of Second City's brand of improv and is now universally employed in workshop and performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In performance contexts, soliciting and incorporating audience input anchors improvisation in spontaneity and shared creation. Guidance includes using suggestions as seeds rather than preplanned material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform teaching into game forms to teach theatrical conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Spolin's Theater Games transform the teaching of acting skills and techniques into exercises that are in game forms; these simple, operational structures teach complicated theater conventions and techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design games so that playing them implicitly trains specific theatrical skills (e.g., listening, focus, status, objectives). The game should operationalize the technique rather than relying on abstract instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design structures that 'fool spontaneity into being'
rubrics_metrics.description: The exercises are described as 'structures designed to almost fool spontaneity into being.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than trying to directly produce spontaneity, create constraints and focuses that make spontaneous choices the natural outcome. Good exercises hide the 'work' behind a playful form so genuine invention can occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use traditional/recreational game structures to unlock creativity and cross-cultural access
rubrics_metrics.description: Spolin adapted focused 'play' and recreational games (influenced by Neva Boyd and WPA work) to unlock the individual's capacity for creative self-expression and to cross the cultural and ethnic barriers of immigrant children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When working in diverse or community settings, use familiar game forms and culturally neutral tasks to make training accessible across backgrounds. Games should be simple, graspable, and transferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume everyone can learn to act (inclusive pedagogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spolin's stated belief: 'Everyone can act. Everyone can improvise... Talent or 'lack of talent' have little to do with it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction should be inclusive and experiential: structure learning so that novices have repeated, safe opportunities to practice and gain confidence, rather than selecting only 'talented' individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience participation and breaking performer/audience separation
rubrics_metrics.description: Spolin organized work (e.g., Game Theater, children's shows) that sought to have audiences participate directly in Theater Games, 'thus effectively eliminating the conventional separation between improvisational actors and audiences.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In pedagogical and performance design, intentionally include formats that invite audience members onto stage or into games to foster communal creativity and reduce performer passivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improv exercises can have therapeutic/sociodramatic effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Spolin acknowledged influence from J.L. Moreno; her exercises had a therapeutic impact on players and drew on psychodrama/sociodrama techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using improv for therapeutic or social-work purposes, be aware of the potential emotional impact and ethical considerations; exercises may be used deliberately to affect social behavior or personal insight and should be facilitated accordingly.
